connection: Session 11 already made ClockEntryRepository's List private, and Employee plus ClockEntry model the core relationship. Reuse that established encapsulation principle while creating TimeSheet composition from the existing models.
objectives: Confirm that ClockEntryRepository's _clockEntries field remains private and explain why callers must use repository methods.
Compare the repository's established private field with ClockEntry's Clockout property, whose private setter also protects mutation.
Read TimeSheet as composition: it owns an Employee and a List<ClockEntry>, and enforces through TryAdd that every stored ClockEntry belongs to its Employee.
Explain why TimeSheet.TryAdd returns false rather than silently accepting a mismatched EmployeeId.

visuals.title: The bypass Session 11 deliberately prevented
visuals.explanation: A public List would let external code call Clear or Add directly. Session 11's private field already closes that route; Session 17 carries the same principle into TimeSheet.

visuals.title: Current state: only repository methods can touch storage
visuals.explanation: Making _clockEntries private forces every interaction through SaveClockEntry, GetClockEntry, and GetEmployeeClockEntries -- exactly the surface IClockEntryRepository already promises.

visuals.title: ClockEntry.Clockout was already encapsulated correctly
visuals.explanation: public DateTime? Clockout { get; private set; } has been this way since Session 6 -- outside callers may read it, but only ClockEntry behavior can assign it.

visuals.title: TimeSheet composes an Employee and a List<ClockEntry>
visuals.explanation: TimeSheet does not inherit from either type -- it owns one Employee and a private list of that employee's ClockEntry objects, exposed only as IReadOnlyList<ClockEntry>.

preQuiz.prompt: What external capability does ClockEntryRepository's private _clockEntries field prevent?
options: Direct access to _clockEntries.Clear(), .Add(...), or indexing from any code outside ClockEntryRepository
preQuiz.explanation: Session 11 already established this boundary: private forces every interaction through repository behavior without exposing the mutable storage object.

preQuiz.prompt: Why was ClockEntry.Clockout never a similar problem, even though it is also a mutable piece of state?
options: Clockout has always had a private setter (public DateTime? Clockout { get; private set; }) -- only ClockOutEntry, a method on ClockEntry itself, can ever change it; there was never a public-field-style bypass to begin with
Clockout is a value type and therefore automatically safe
Clockout is read-only and can never change
preQuiz.explanation: Both designs control mutation differently: the repository hides its field, while ClockEntry exposes a readable property whose setter remains private.

preQuiz.prompt: Why does TimeSheet.TryAdd return false when a ClockEntry's EmployeeId doesn't match the TimeSheet's Employee?
options: A TimeSheet's whole reason for existing is grouping one employee's entries together -- false reports the expected rejection while preserving that invariant
Every Try method in C# is required to compare EmployeeId
It has no real reason -- it is arbitrary
preQuiz.explanation: The Try-pattern was introduced earlier: true means the entry was accepted and false means it was rejected. Exception-design judgment arrives later, so this session uses an already-understood contract.

concept.title: Three declarations protect three different boundaries
paragraphs: The field and property work together, but private, readonly, and IReadOnlyList<ClockEntry> do different jobs. None of the three keywords or types replaces the others.

The List itself remains mutable inside TimeSheet. readonly prevents assigning _entries to a different List after initialization; it does not freeze the current List or prevent TimeSheet.TryAdd from calling _entries.Add.

rows: Outside callers cannot directly access or mutate _entries.
TimeSheet cannot reassign the field after initialization; the existing List can still be mutated internally.
Callers can count, index, and enumerate through Entries, but the public contract has no Add, Remove, or Clear.
Would expose mutation methods and let callers bypass TryAdd's ownership check.

concept.code:
private readonly List<ClockEntry> _entries = new();
public IReadOnlyList<ClockEntry> Entries => _entries;

concept.title: Reuse the repository boundary Session 11 already established
paragraphs: ClockEntryRepository already declares private readonly List<ClockEntry> _clockEntries, exactly as Session 11 instructed. Its methods can mutate that field because they belong to the class; outside callers cannot reach the field.

Session 17 does not edit the repository. It uses the repository as a known example: mutable storage stays private, and a smaller public surface controls how state changes. TimeSheet applies the same rule to its own List<ClockEntry>.

concept.title: Contrast: ClockEntry.Clockout was correct from the start
paragraphs: ClockEntry's constructor and ClockOutEntry have not changed since Session 6 -- Clockout's private setter already prevented exactly the kind of external bypass _clockEntries just had.
Seeing a private field (ClockEntryRepository) and a public property with a private setter (ClockEntry) side by side makes two different encapsulation techniques concrete.
concept.code: public DateTime? Clockout { get; private set; }   // correct since Session 6 -- never needed fixing

concept.title: TimeSheet: composition with an enforced ownership rule
paragraphs: TimeSheet owns an Employee (assigned once in its constructor) and a private List<ClockEntry> exposed only as IReadOnlyList<ClockEntry>. Callers can read Entries but cannot call Add through that public contract; they must go through TimeSheet.TryAdd.
TryAdd checks entry.EmployeeId against Employee.Identity before mutating the list. A matching entry is added and returns true; a mismatched entry leaves the list unchanged and returns false.

concept.title: IReadOnlyList protects the public route to the collection
paragraphs: TimeSheet still needs a real List<ClockEntry> internally because TryAdd mutates it. Its public Entries property uses IReadOnlyList<ClockEntry>, which permits Count, indexing, and enumeration but does not declare Add, Remove, or Clear.
The declared public type is the important contract: normal callers cannot bypass TryAdd through Entries. This continues Session 13's principle of exposing only the capabilities a caller needs.

lab.objective: Apply an established encapsulation pattern by creating a TimeSheet that owns one Employee and accepts only that employee's ClockEntry objects.
lab.startingCondition: ClockEntryRepository already keeps its List private. Employee and ClockEntry exist, but no TimeSheet groups one employee with a protected entry collection.
lab.keyPointTitle: The field and property protect different things
keyPoints: private prevents outside callers from directly accessing _entries.
readonly prevents field reassignment; it does not make the List contents immutable, so TimeSheet can still call _entries.Add internally.
IReadOnlyList<ClockEntry> lets callers count, index, and enumerate Entries without exposing Add, Remove, or Clear.
Returning List<ClockEntry> would let callers bypass TryAdd and violate the one-employee ownership rule.
lab.keyPointCode:
private readonly List<ClockEntry> _entries = new();
public IReadOnlyList<ClockEntry> Entries => _entries;

Confirm that SaveClockEntry, GetClockEntry, and GetEmployeeClockEntries can still access the private field because they belong to the same class.

Declare a public sealed TimeSheet class.

Stub a constructor that requires one Employee. The TimeSheet-to-Employee relationship is established once during construction.

steps: Declare a public get-only Employee property.

steps.text: Expose the entries through IReadOnlyList<ClockEntry>. This public contract permits reading and indexing but does not expose Add, Remove, or Clear.

steps: Build now, before creating TryAdd, to confirm the private field and public read-only collection contract compile together.

steps.text: Stub TryAdd. Its Boolean result will report whether the entry belongs to this TimeSheet's Employee.

steps: Build again to confirm the TimeSheet structure and method contracts compile.
Replace the constructor throw by assigning the employee parameter to the Employee property.
Replace the throw in TryAdd with a comparison between entry.EmployeeId and Employee.Identity.
Return false immediately when the IDs do not match.
Add the entry to _entries only after the ownership check succeeds.
Return true after adding the matching entry.
Explain why the EmployeeId check must occur before _entries.Add: rejected data must never enter the protected collection.
Open App/Program.cs.
Keep every earlier application section unchanged.
Add a clearly labeled Session 17 section at the end of Program.cs.
Create one Employee to own the TimeSheet.
Construct a TimeSheet using that employee.

postQuiz.prompt: Why did Session 11's private _clockEntries field require no changes to IClockEntryRepository or any of its method signatures?
options: The interface never exposed the field in the first place -- SaveClockEntry, GetClockEntry, and GetEmployeeClockEntries were always the intended public surface; only the field's accidental public visibility needed correcting
IClockEntryRepository was also changed as part of the fix
It required changes to every class implementing IClockEntryRepository
postQuiz.explanation: The interface describes callable behavior, not private storage. Changing an implementation detail's visibility does not alter that public contract.

postQuiz.prompt: Could TimeSheet have used inheritance (TimeSheet : Employee) instead of composition (TimeSheet owning an Employee) to associate an employee with their entries?
options: No -- a TimeSheet is not a kind of Employee (inheritance's 'is-a' relationship doesn't hold); it HAS an Employee, which is exactly what composition ('has-a') models
Yes -- inheritance and composition are interchangeable here
Only if Employee were declared abstract
postQuiz.explanation: This is the classic is-a versus has-a distinction: TimeSheet has an Employee and a list of that employee's entries -- it is not itself a more specific kind of Employee.

postQuiz.prompt: What would happen if TimeSheet.Entries returned List<ClockEntry> instead of IReadOnlyList<ClockEntry>?
options: Callers could call Entries.Add(...) or Entries.Clear() directly, bypassing TimeSheet.TryAdd's EmployeeId-matching check entirely
Nothing would change -- List<T> and IReadOnlyList<T> expose identical members
The code would fail to compile
postQuiz.explanation: IReadOnlyList<T> deliberately omits Add/Remove/Clear -- returning the narrower interface is what protects TimeSheet's own invariant, the same principle Session 13 covered for GetEmployeeClockEntries.

reflections: How do ClockEntryRepository's private field and ClockEntry.Clockout's private setter protect mutation in different ways?
What would you check for, in a code review, to catch a class exposing a mutable field the way ClockEntryRepository originally did?
How does TimeSheet's IReadOnlyList<ClockEntry> return type connect back to Session 13's discussion of interface-level promises?
whatBreaks: Changing the already-private _clockEntries field to public would create a bypass: any caller with a ClockEntryRepository reference could clear or directly mutate stored entries. Returning TimeSheet's mutable List directly would create the same kind of bypass around TryAdd's EmployeeId validation.
summary: Session 11's private repository field remains unchanged and provides the pattern for this session. ClockEntry.Clockout's private setter is another established example. TimeSheet applies the same encapsulation principle through composition: it owns an Employee and a private list, exposes a narrower IReadOnlyList contract, and uses TryAdd to preserve employee-entry ownership.
